headline: Pennsylvania Now Requires Labels on AI-Made Ads

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Pennsylvania has a new rule for advertisements. An advertisement, or "ad," is something companies make to get people to buy their products, like a commercial on TV or a flyer for a restaurant. Some ads are now made using artificial intelligence, or "AI," which is computer technology that can create pictures, videos, sounds, or words almost like a person would. The new rule says that if an ad was made or changed a lot using AI, it must have a label telling people that. This way, people watching or reading the ad know a computer helped make it, not just a real person or real footage. The governor of Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro, signed this rule into law. It applies to big companies and small businesses alike, even a restaurant's flyer about chicken wings. However, the rule has some gray areas. It does not apply to jokes, parodies, or things that are clearly pretend. It is also not totally clear how much an ad needs to be changed by AI before it needs a label. This law is one of the first of its kind in the United States.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Pennsylvania just passed a new law that affects how companies can advertise. Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, which means any ad that is created or heavily changed using artificial intelligence (AI) must include a clear label saying so. This applies to all kinds of ads: TV commercials, pictures, audio clips, written text, and even paper flyers for local businesses. The label has to match the style of the ad itself, so a video ad needs a video label, and a text ad needs a text label. This matters because AI can now create very realistic images, voices, and videos that look real but aren't. Without labels, people might be tricked into thinking something is genuine when it was actually generated by a computer program. Pennsylvania is one of the very first states to pass a law like this. Interestingly, the law applies no matter where the ad was actually made, so if a company wants their ad to air in Pennsylvania, they have to follow this rule even if their business is based somewhere else. That means people in other states might start seeing these labels too. However, the law isn't perfectly clear in every way. It doesn't define exactly what counts as an ad being "significantly modified" by AI. It also allows exceptions for jokes, satire, or things that are obviously not real, but it doesn't clearly explain what counts as "obviously not real." Because of these unclear parts, companies and lawmakers may argue over how to follow the law in the future.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed a new law called the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act. This law requires companies to label any advertisement that has been significantly created or changed using artificial intelligence (AI), a type of computer technology that can generate realistic images, videos, audio, and text. The label must appear in the same format as the ad—meaning a video ad needs a visible or spoken disclosure, and a printed flyer needs a written one. This rule applies broadly, covering everything from expensive national TV commercials to a small restaurant's flyer advertising a wing special. Pennsylvania is one of the first states in the country to pass legislation like this, making it a notable example other states might follow. One interesting detail is that the law applies based on where an ad is shown, not where it was made. This means a company based in another state could still be required to add an AI disclosure if its ad is meant to air in Pennsylvania. As a result, people living outside Pennsylvania might start noticing these AI labels too, since companies often use the same ad across multiple states rather than making separate versions. This law exists because AI-generated content has become realistic enough to potentially mislead consumers. For example, an ad might use an AI-generated voice or face that looks and sounds like a real person, even though it was never actually recorded. Lawmakers want to make sure people know when they're seeing something artificially created so they aren't deceived into trusting it the way they would trust real footage or testimony. However, the law contains several unclear areas, sometimes called "loopholes." First, it doesn't precisely define what counts as an ad being "significantly modified" by AI, leaving room for different interpretations. Second, the law doesn't require labels for parody, satire, commentary, or content that is "evidently fictional"—but it never explains what makes something clearly fictional enough to skip the label. Finally, the law seems to require disclosure mainly when AI content creates a "false consumer perception," meaning it tricks people in some way, but it doesn't specify exactly what counts as false or who decides that. Because of these gaps, businesses, regulators, and courts may need to sort out exactly how the law should be enforced in real situations.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Pennsylvania has become one of the first states in the country to legally require disclosure labels on AI-generated advertisements. Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, mandating that any advertisement—whether a still image, video, audio clip, or block of text—must carry a visible or audible disclosure if it has been "significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence." The disclosure must appear in the same format as the ad itself, meaning video ads need video-format labels and printed materials need printed labels. The law is sweeping in scope, covering everything from major national TV commercials produced by billion-dollar corporations to a local restaurant's hand-made flyer advertising a food special. Notably, the law applies based on where an advertisement is intended to be shown rather than where it was created. This means a business located anywhere in the country could be required to add a Pennsylvania-compliant disclosure if its ad is meant to reach Pennsylvania audiences. Since companies frequently reuse the same advertisement across multiple states rather than creating state-specific versions, this law could effectively push AI disclosure labels into advertising seen well beyond Pennsylvania's borders. The motivation behind this legislation is rooted in growing concern over how convincingly AI can now mimic real people, voices, and footage. As AI tools become capable of producing highly realistic synthetic media, there's increasing risk that audiences could be deceived into believing an ad features real people, real events, or authentic testimonials when it does not. By requiring clear labeling, lawmakers hope to preserve consumer trust and allow people to make informed judgments about what they're seeing. Despite its ambitious goals, the law contains significant ambiguities that could complicate enforcement. For instance, the law does not clearly define what qualifies as an ad being "significantly modified" by AI—leaving open questions about how much AI alteration triggers the labeling requirement. The law also exempts content meant as parody, satire, commentary, or criticism, as well as material that is "evidently fictional," but offers no clear standard for what counts as obviously fictional. Perhaps most importantly, the law appears to require disclosure specifically when AI-generated content creates a "false consumer perception" about a product or service—yet it doesn't explain what qualifies as false or who has the authority to make that determination. These unresolved questions suggest that regulators, businesses, and potentially courts will need to interpret and refine the law's practical application over time, especially as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Pennsylvania has positioned itself at the forefront of AI regulation in advertising by enacting the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, signed into law by Governor Josh Shapiro. The statute mandates that any advertisement—spanning still images, video, audio, or text—must include a disclosure label if it has been "significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence." Crucially, the required label must match the medium of the ad itself, meaning a video advertisement needs a video-based disclosure while printed materials require a written one. The law's reach is notably broad, applying equally to polished television commercials from multinational corporations and to modest printed flyers produced by local restaurants. One of the law's most consequential provisions is that its applicability depends on where an advertisement is intended to be viewed, not where it originates. Consequently, businesses operating anywhere in the United States could find themselves obligated to comply if their advertising is slated to appear in Pennsylvania. Because national advertising campaigns are typically distributed identically across multiple states rather than customized region by region, this jurisdictional approach means Pennsylvania's disclosure requirement could realistically shape advertising content seen by audiences nationwide—giving a single state's law outsized national influence, a pattern seen before with other state-level regulations. The legislation reflects mounting concern about the advertising industry's growing use of generative AI tools capable of producing highly convincing synthetic images, voices, and video. As this technology becomes more sophisticated and harder to distinguish from authentic recordings, regulators worry that consumers could be misled into believing they are viewing real people, genuine testimonials, or unaltered footage, when in fact the content was artificially generated or substantially altered. By mandating clear, format-matched disclosures, lawmakers aim to preserve a baseline level of consumer trust and transparency in commercial messaging. Nevertheless, the law's language leaves considerable room for interpretation, which could complicate enforcement and compliance. The statute does not define a concrete threshold for what constitutes "significant" modification by AI, leaving businesses and regulators to determine case by case whether a given use of AI editing tools triggers the disclosure requirement. The law also carves out exemptions for parody, satire, commentary, and criticism, as well as content that is "evidently fictional"—yet it offers no objective criteria for what makes fictional content sufficiently "evident" to qualify for exemption. Perhaps most significantly, the law's requirement appears tied to whether AI-generated content creates a "false consumer perception" regarding a product or service, but it does not specify what standard determines falsity or which party—regulators, courts, or consumers themselves—bears responsibility for making that judgment. These ambiguities suggest that the practical scope and enforcement of the law will likely be shaped through future regulatory guidance, litigation, or amendment, particularly as AI-generated advertising content continues to proliferate and grow more sophisticated across industries.

questions: If you saw a TV commercial that used an AI-generated voice or face, would knowing that change how much you trust the ad? Why or why not?
Do you think it should matter where an ad is shown versus where it was made when deciding whether a law applies to it? How might this affect businesses in other states?

The law doesn't clearly define words like 'significantly modified' or 'evidently fictional.' Why might it be hard to write a law about new technology like AI, and how could unclear rules cause problems?
